summary: This RFC describes the Host-Front End Protocol in detail, as a proposal and not a final standard, and asks readers to test implementations and coordinate with the author. It is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: A big computer lets a front helper handle the network work. This is the full rule book, offered as a draft to try out.

subtitle: A draft protocol that lets a host hand its networking work to an outboard front end through a small set of text commands.

tldr.problem: Running every network protocol inside each host costs CPU cycles and memory, and writing implementations for many kinds of host is hard to arrange.
tldr.mechanism: The Host-Front End Protocol (H-FP) lets a host process drive protocol interpreters in an outboard processing environment (OPE) using seven ASCII commands, each answered by a three-digit response code, over a reliable channel.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is a proposal for a standard, not a standard, and an unfinished one. It is marked Historic.

today: The unit metadata marks RFC 929 as Historic and lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The RFC itself calls H-FP a proposal for a standard, and points to RFC 928 as its introduction.

sections.title: A Proposal for Outboard Protocol Processing
sections.content:
RFC 929 describes the Host-Front End Protocol (H-FP). It opens with a warning: it is a proposal for a standard, not a standard, and it assumes the reader has already read RFC 928, its introduction. The authors also say it is unfinished. Appendices for most offloaded protocols were not yet written, the response codes probably need clarification and expansion, and the plan was to revise the protocol based on experience from volunteer test implementations.

The RFC names two motivations for outboard processing. One is to conserve the hosts' resources (CPU cycles and memory) by moving as much networking software as possible into an Outboard Processing Environment (OPE), also called a network front-end. The other is to make it easier to obtain implementations of the many protocols for the several types of host in a heterogeneous network, by using common implementations in the OPE.
sections.plainLanguage: A busy grown-up hands the phone calls to an assistant. The assistant does the talking to the outside, so the grown-up has more time for other work.

sections.title: Three Layers and the Conceptual Model
sections.content:
An H-FP resolves into three layers. The Link layer exchanges bits between host and OPE. The Channel layer demultiplexes the bit streams and provides flow control per stream. The Command (or Service Access) layer is the RFC's main concern, and is what the RFC calls "the H-FP". It lets host processes manipulate protocol interpreters (PIs) in the OPE on their behalf.

The Channel layer carries data in units called chunks; on an X.25 channel a chunk would be a packet. Each data stream is fully asynchronous, and the Channel service must be reliable: correct order, no duplication, checked for bit errors, with retransmission and duplicate detection hidden from the user. Channel flow control is also what replaces explicit events such as the Allocate event of the TCP interface in MIL-STD 1778, so such events need not be sent at the Command level.

The model is a closed subroutine interface between a host process and a PI that happens to be outboard. If the protocols were inboard, the calling process would not know the difference.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three jobs: a road between the two machines, a traffic cop that keeps separate conversations apart, and the actual requests. This memo is mostly about the requests.

sections.title: Command and Response Syntax
sections.content:
Commands and responses are written in ASCII characters. The RFC lists reasons: most hosts can generate and read ASCII, test scripts are easy to write, an OPE can act as a simple virtual terminal during development, and a terminal or data line analyzer is enough for testing.

The first character of each chunk says how it is used: C for one complete command, F for the first part of a multichunk command, M for a middle part and L for the last. So <C>, <F><L> and <F><M><M><L> are legal, while <L>, <M><L> and <F><C> are not.

The command name is at least its first two letters in either case (BE or be for Begin). Parameters follow, separated by one or more spaces, and their order matters. A parameter can be skipped with ,, or named with a short flag such as -p. A newline outside a quoted string ends the command, and any data follows it, padded with spaces so it starts on a word boundary.

A response is a special command named RE, followed by the original command identifier, a three-digit response code, protocol idiosyncratic parameters and a text message that humans can read but that is not required.
sections.plainLanguage: Every message is plain typed words. The first letter says if it is a whole message or one piece of a long one, and the rest says what to do.

sections.title: The Seven Commands
sections.content:
The commands are Begin, Transmit, Signal, Condition, Status, End and No-op. Either the host or the OPE may issue them, though some only make sense in one direction.

  • Begin starts communication between a host process and an offloaded protocol interpreter. Its parameters include the protocol (such as TCP, UDP, IP, TEL, FTP or SMTP), active or passive, two-part addresses, a mediation level and type of service advice.
  • Transmit sends data through the interpreter, or delivers data that arrived from the network.
  • Signal carries an out-of-band signal.
  • Condition changes characteristics that Begin set up.
  • Status requests or reports status.
  • End says services are no longer needed, either gracefully (G) or abruptly (A).
  • No-op does nothing and supports testing.

The dialog is lock step: the issuer of a command waits for its response before issuing another. The exceptions are the abrupt End, which can be sent at any time, and Signal, which can be sent while other commands are pending but should not precede a successful response to Begin.

The mediation level is one digit from 0 (no OPE mediation) to 9 (full OPE mediation, the default). The Transmit response discipline is N (respond once the command is checked, the default) or B (respond only after the data is transmitted).
sections.plainLanguage: There are only seven kinds of request, like open, send, wave, change, ask, stop and are-you-there. Each time you ask, you wait for the answer before asking again.

sections.title: Response Codes
sections.content:
Every response carries a three-digit code. The first digit gives the group and the last two digits qualify it. Groups run from 0XX success to 6XX security problems, with 7XX and 8XX reserved and 9XX used for errors idiosyncratic to the offloaded protocol.

Each command lists its own responses. For Begin they include 000 (completed), 302 (protocol not supported), 304 (passive service not available), 402 (remote protocol interpreter not available) and 501 (insufficient OPE resources). The authors say the codes almost certainly need clarification and expansion.
sections.plainLanguage: Each answer starts with a number. The first digit says whether things went well or what kind of trouble happened.

sections.title: Offloading TCP and Telnet
sections.content:
The appendix shows the commands in use for TCP and Telnet. For TCP it maps the requests and responses of the MIL-STD 1778 interface onto H-FP commands: passive and active opens become Begin commands, Send becomes Transmit, and Close and Abort become the graceful and abrupt forms of End. Status uses the query form of the Status command.

An example from the main text is a Begin issued by an inboard Telnet interpreter to open a TCP connection to the host ISIA with no timeout. The appendix sections for FTP, mail and other protocols are marked TBS, meaning to be supplied.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo shows how opening a phone-style connection to another computer turns into one short typed line to the helper box.
